published.title: ESMA consults on reporting framework for clearing activity at recognised third-country CCPs
published.title_original: ESMA consults on reporting framework for clearing activity at recognised third-country CCPs
published.summary_original: ESMA consults on reporting framework for clearing activity at recognised third-country CCPs 18 August 2026 CCP Simplification and Burden Reduction The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU's financial markets regulator and supervisor, has launched a consultation on a proposed annual reporting framework under EMIR for clearing activity at recognised third-country central counterparties (CCPs), aimed at improving supervisory visibility of EU firms' exposures to such CCPs. The consultation paper sets out ESMA's proposed Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) and Implementing Technical Standards (ITS) under European Market Infrastructure Regulation (EMIR). The reporting obligation will apply to clearing members and clients that clear transactions through recognised third country CCPs. The objective is to provide supervisory authorities with a structured and consistent overview of the scale, characteristics and risk profile of EU firms' exposures to recognised third-country CCPs, contributing to the broader monitoring framework established under EMIR 3. In line with ESMA’s simplification and burden reduction agenda, the proposal seeks to maximise the reuse of informatio
published.why_kept: Luxembourg banks and investment firms using recognised third-country CCPs may be directly subject to the future EMIR reporting requirements.
published.summary: ESMA is consulting on proposed RTS and ITS establishing an annual reporting framework under EMIR for clearing activity at recognised third-country CCPs. The framework would improve supervisory visibility of EU firms’ exposures and could require affected firms to implement new reporting processes, data controls and technical submissions.
published.actions: Assess exposure to recognised third-country CCPs, review the proposed RTS and ITS, identify required data and reporting controls, and prepare for implementation if adopted.

published.title: ESMA confirms go-live for weekly commodity derivatives position reporting
published.title_original: ESMA confirms go-live for weekly commodity derivatives position reporting
published.summary_original: ESMA confirms go-live for weekly commodity derivatives position reporting 14 August 2026 Trading The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA), the EU’s financial markets regulator and supervisor, announces that the new weekly commodity derivatives position reporting framework will go live on 3 September 2026. From this date, market participants will be required to submit weekly position reports in accordance with the updated requirements, technical specifications and validation rules introduced by XML schema version v2.0. Following ESMA's original announcement and the decision to postpone the rollout , additional time has been dedicated to technical and operational preparations to support a smooth transition to the new reporting arrangements. The updated technical documentation ( reporting instructions and XML schema ) is now available to support market participants in completing their implementation activities. Further information: Cristina Bonillo Senior Communications Officer press@esma.europa.eu 14/08/2026 ESMA65-955014868-14991 Commodities derivatives weekly position reporting - Reporting instructions 14/08/2026 ESMA65-955014868-14993 XML Schema for commodities derivat
published.why_kept: Luxembourg investment firms active in commodity derivatives or reporting on behalf of market participants may need to meet the EU-wide reporting requirements.
published.summary: ESMA confirms that the updated weekly commodity derivatives position-reporting framework will go live on 2026-09-03, using XML schema version 2.0 and revised technical specifications and validation rules. Market participants must be technically and operationally ready to submit reports under the updated requirements.
published.actions: Update reporting systems to XML schema v2.0, validate data and controls against the revised specifications, complete testing, and ensure operational readiness for submissions from the go-live date.

published.title: EBA ESG risk dashboard shows stable climate risk exposures and continued improvements in data quality
published.title_original: EBA ESG risk dashboard shows stable climate risk exposures and continued improvements in data quality
published.summary_original: The European Banking Authority (EBA) today published its latest Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) risk dashboard, showing continued stability in banks’ transition and physical climate risk indicators across the EU/EEA in second half of 2025. The results also indicate gradual improvements in the availability and quality of climate-related data, particularly for energy efficiency assessments of mortgage portfolios, supporting more robust climate risk monitoring in the banking sector.
published.why_kept: Luxembourg credit institutions may be assessed against the same EU supervisory expectations concerning climate-risk data, governance and risk management.

published.title_original: ​The EBA consults on draft technical standards on institutions’ operational risk management
published.summary_original: ​The European Banking Authority (EBA) today launched a public consultation on draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) specifying the operational risk management framework that institutions must have in place as per Article 323 of the Capital Requirements Regulation (CRR3). The draft RTS set out harmonised, proportionate requirements for the governance, management process and systems institutions should use to identify, assess, monitor and manage operational risk. The consultation runs until 31 December 2026.
published.why_kept: Luxembourg credit institutions and in-scope investment firms will need to prepare for the harmonised CRR3 operational-risk management requirements and may wish to contribute to the consultation.
published.summary: The EBA has launched a consultation on draft Regulatory Technical Standards under Article 323 of CRR3 concerning institutions’ operational risk management frameworks. The draft RTS would harmonise proportionate expectations for governance, operational-risk management processes, and the systems used to identify, assess, monitor and manage operational risk. The consultation is open to institutions and other stakeholders until 31 December 2026.
published.actions: Review the draft RTS against the institution’s operational-risk framework, governance, policies, systems and controls; identify implementation gaps; and submit consultation feedback by the closing date if appropriate.

published.title: The EBA consults on revised technical standards for the reclassification of investment firms as credit institutions
published.title_original: The EBA consults on revised technical standards for the reclassification of investment firms as credit institutions
published.summary_original: The European Banking Authority (EBA) today launched a consultation on three draft Regulatory Technical Standards (RTS) on the reclassification of investment firms as credit institutions, when they exceed the EUR 30 billion total assets threshold. The proposals clarify how total assets should be calculated against this threshold, how investment firms should report this information to competent authorities, and the conditions under which competent authorities can decide to grant a waiver. The revised RTS reflect the 2024 amendments to the Capital Requirements Directive (CRD) and contribute to a more proportionate and risk-based application of the framework for investment firms. The consultation is open until 25 November 2026.
published.why_kept: Luxembourg investment firms approaching the threshold may need to assess their asset calculations, reporting processes and potential transition to the credit-institution framework.
published.summary: The EBA is consulting on three draft RTS clarifying when investment firms exceeding EUR 30 billion in total assets must be reclassified as credit institutions under the amended CRD framework. The proposals address the calculation of total assets, reporting to competent authorities and waiver conditions, with practical implications for firms approaching the threshold and their prudential classification.
published.actions: Monitor the consultation and assess the impact of the proposed asset-calculation, reporting and waiver requirements on the firm’s prudential status.

published.title: AIFM’s Valuation Framework
published.title_original: AIFM’s Valuation Framework
published.summary_original: This project aims to strengthen and formalise the AIFM’s valuation framework by introducing a coherent and structured set of tools covering both governance and execution. It consists of 3 complementary components: a valuation memo defining key principles, expectations and controls. This document was first issued in May 2026 and has been updated in September 2026 to reflect relevant considerations from the CSSF Thematic Review – Valuation Framework for Less Liquid and Illiquid Assets (June 2026) ; a valuation tracker providing quarterly visibility on valuation-related efforts, issues and follow-up actions, and; a valuation analysis template ensuring consistent, well-documented and challengeable valuation assessments at asset level. Together, these tools are expected to enhance transparency, traceability and consistency across valuation processes, support effective challenge by independent functions, and ensure alignment with regulatory expectations, while remaining proportionate to the AIFM’s size, strategies and asset classes.
published.why_kept: Luxembourg AIFMs and alternative investment structures commonly handle less liquid assets and should be able to demonstrate robust, documented and independently challengeable valuation processes.
published.summary: The LPEA project strengthens and formalises the valuation framework used by AIFMs through a valuation memo, a quarterly valuation tracker and a valuation analysis template. It addresses governance, execution, documentation and challengeability, and reflects considerations from the CSSF thematic review of less liquid and illiquid asset valuations.
published.actions: Assess the existing valuation framework against the memo, tracker and template; assign governance responsibilities; document valuation decisions and exceptions; and implement periodic follow-up of outstanding valuation issues.

published.title: Learning probability of default and stress testing
published.title_original: Learning probability of default and stress testing
published.summary_original: We analyze the Probability of Default (PD) of non-financial corporations in Europe using Random Forests (RF) and assess implications for stress testing the banking sector. To this end, we exploit data on firms’ financial statements (Orbis) and banks’ credit registry (Anacredit). We show that RF displays stronger risk sensitivity than logistic regression in stress testing, shedding new light on the non-linear effect of scenario severity on PD. Moreover, we show how RF-based PD can be used in a network of banks and firms to stress test the banking sector through loan exposures as a key transmission channel of adverse scenarios. A granular inspection of banks’ riskiness indices derived from this network sheds light also on RF’s superior ability in capturing non-linearity thanks to its capability in identifying “tail banks”. Our work is relevant for central banks and banking supervisors alike.
published.why_kept: The analysis may inform Luxembourg banks’ credit-risk modelling, validation and stress-testing methodologies, particularly where machine-learning approaches are being considered.
published.summary: This ECB research paper evaluates Random Forest models for estimating corporate probability of default and applying the results to bank stress testing. It examines whether machine-learning techniques capture nonlinear risk effects and transmission through bank-firm lending exposures, but does not introduce binding requirements.
published.actions: Review the findings as relevant to model-development, validation and stress-testing practices; no immediate regulatory filing or implementation is required.

published.summary_original: On 01 September 2026, the LPEA submitted its response to the AMLA Public Consultation on Draft Guidelines on ongoing monitoring of a business relationship under Article 26(5) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1624. The Association emphasised the importance of preserving a risk-based and proportionate approach to AML/CFT obligations for alternative asset management companies. It highlighted the need for sufficient flexibility in the implementation of mitigation measures that are commensurate to the actual risk, as envisaged by Section 3.2 “AMLA’s approach” of the draft guidelines, allowing professionals to take into account sector-specific characteristics, the inherent risk profile of Alternative Investment Funds, and their own risk assessments. The LPEA also underlined that overly prescriptive requirements could create unnecessary burdens, undermine the competitiveness of the EU financial centre, and risk the unintended exclusion of certain geographies, industries, or investor groups from financial services. published.title: Banks’ funding structures and pass-through in the euro area
published.title_original: Banks’ funding structures and pass-through in the euro area
published.summary_original: This paper investigates the interest rate pass-through of monetary policy in the euro area by focusing on the role of banks’ funding structures. We estimate the interest rate pass-through for loans to non-financial corporations using bank-level balance sheet data. In doing so, we interact the response of lending rates with characteristics of the funding structure, and show that banks that rely more on bond issuance than on the money market tend to be less responsive to policy changes. Finally, we test the presence of the asset-liability-management channel, and find that banks combining longer-term liabilities (higher bond shares) with longer rate fixation periods for loans (higher share of loans with fixed rates) exhibit the most muted lending rate response to policy shocks.
published.why_kept: The findings are relevant to Luxembourg banks’ funding, asset-liability-management and interest-rate risk assessments.
published.summary: An ECB research paper examines how euro-area banks’ funding structures affect the transmission of monetary policy to lending rates. It analyses bank-level data and finds that reliance on bond funding and longer-term liabilities can reduce the responsiveness of lending rates to policy changes.

published.title: The use of the Eurosystem’s monetary policy instruments and its monetary policy implementation framework in 2024 and 2025
published.title_original: The use of the Eurosystem’s monetary policy instruments and its monetary policy implementation framework in 2024 and 2025
published.summary_original: The Eurosystem implements its monetary policy through a set of monetary policy instruments (MPIs). This report reviews the main changes in the use of MPIs and the associated developments in the Eurosystem’s monetary policy implementation framework over 2024-25. Inflation returned to the ECB’s medium-term target of 2%, supported by the smooth transmission of monetary policy. After completing the hiking cycle of 2022 and 2023, the ECB began reducing its key interest rates in June 2024. This easing phase occurred alongside further balance sheet normalisation. Holdings in the monetary policy bond portfolios continued to run-off, and funds lent under the third series of targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTRO III) were fully repaid by December 2024. In March 2024, the ECB announced several changes to its operational framework for implementing monetary policy following a review process. Finally, the collateral framework remained broad, while temporary crisis-related measures were phased out and climate-related considerations were further integrated.
published.why_kept: Luxembourg credit institutions may need to assess the effects of changes in Eurosystem refinancing conditions, interest rates and central-bank liquidity operations.
published.summary: This ECB report reviews how the Eurosystem used its monetary policy instruments and how its monetary policy implementation framework evolved during 2024 and 2025. It covers the shift from monetary tightening to easing, reductions in key interest rates, balance-sheet normalisation and the continued run-off of monetary policy bond portfolios, with implications for banks’ liquidity and funding conditions.
published.actions: Monitor the ECB’s monetary policy implementation framework and assess implications for liquidity planning, funding costs, collateral and interest-rate risk.

pending_review.title: When the Crowd Speaks: AI-based retail investor sentiment indicator with Reddit data
pending_review.title_original: When the Crowd Speaks: AI-based retail investor sentiment indicator with Reddit data
pending_review.summary_original: Retail investors increasingly discuss markets in real time on social media, yet these discussions remain difficult to measure systematically. This paper introduces the Reddit Retail Investor Sentiment Indicator (R-RISI), a high-frequency measure of retail investor sentiment based on Reddit posts from major investing and crypto-related subreddits between 2015 and April 2026. Using ChatGPT 5.1, we classify posts by sentiment and topic and show that large language models provide more accurate labels for informal social media language than widely used finance-specific models such as FinBERT, which tends to over-assign neutral sentiment. R-RISI is constructed by aggregating daily positive and negative posts, weighting them by user engagement and standardising the resulting series using a rolling one-year z-score methodology. The indicator can be flexibly built for broad asset classes, portfolios, individual securities or thematic groups, allowing sentiment to be tracked at a much higher granularity than traditional retail investor indicators. We show how sentiment and dominant discussion topics evolve over time within each of the extracted subreddits. R-RISI closely reflects major marke
pending_review.why_kept: The study is relevant to Luxembourg investment and crypto-market participants assessing investor behaviour, market-monitoring tools and the governance risks of AI-generated market intelligence.
pending_review.summary: This ECB research paper presents an AI-based indicator of retail investor sentiment derived from Reddit discussions about financial markets and crypto-related topics. It assesses the use of large language models to classify sentiment and topics in high-frequency social-media data; it is analytical rather than a binding regulatory measure.

rejected.summary_original: The FCA has decided to ban 3 former senior figures at Dolfin Financial (UK) Limited (Dolfin) after finding they ran a scheme that helped clients bypass UK visa rules. Former chief executive Denisz Nagy has been fined £324,800 and former finance director Sanjay Maraj £122,000 for their roles in the scheme. Both have been banned from working in financial services. The FCA has also decided to ban Dolfin co-founder, Roman Joukovski, from working in financial services. Between 2016 and 2019, most clients using the scheme paid a fee of £400,000 instead of investing £2m of their own money in UK companies, as required under the Home Office investor visa rules. The FCA found the scheme was deliberately designed to create the false impression that the visa requirements had been met. The scheme enabled at least 99 individuals to obtain investor visas and generated at least £35.5m in fees for Dolfin-connected businesses and the immigration agents that introduced clients.The FCA found that Mr Nagy and Mr Joukovski played leading roles in creating and operating the scheme, while Mr Maraj was responsible for the financial aspects once it was set up. rejected.title: Hidden in the aggregate: the cyclicality of EU labour force participation
rejected.title_original: Hidden in the aggregate: the cyclicality of EU labour force participation
rejected.summary_original: We estimate the cyclical response of labour force participation to growth shocks across EU regions. We use a shift-share instrumental variable approach and local projections on EU Labour Force Survey microdata covering 15 countries and 114 regions over 2000–2020. The aggregate labour force participation rate is remarkably resilient, a clear contrast to the highly cyclical participation rate documented for the U.S. However, this resilience masks pronounced demographic heterogeneity. Men’s participation declines significantly while women’s remains stable, reflecting sectoral segregation and the added worker effect. Young workers exhibit the most persistent responses, with effects lasting up to eight years, consistent with hysteresis through human capital erosion. Less-educated and non-native workers bear disproportionate employment costs. The findings imply that aggregate slack measures may miss important distributional dimensions relevant for monetary, fiscal, and structural policy.

rejected.title_original: Can structural reforms unleash private investment?
rejected.summary_original: This paper examines the impact of labour and product market reforms on private investment across 26 advanced economies from 1975 to 2020. To this end, we combine a narrative database on major structural reforms with local projections and augmented inverse probability weighting. We find that a major labour market reform typically increases the level of real private investment by 5% cumulatively within six years, while a major product market reform yields an impact of 3%. Structural reforms are particularly effective in stimulating private investment when the private sector has access to ample external finance and the rule of law is strong. Overall, our findings point to an important role for structural reforms in boosting private investment and thus long-term growth prospects in advanced economies.

rejected.title_original: Monetary policy and the rigidity of firm employment expectations
rejected.summary_original: This paper examines how monetary policy announcements affect firms’ employment expectations. Using German survey data, we combine high-frequency monetary policy surprises with survey response dates to identify the immediate and dynamic effects of monetary policy on firm-level expectations and subsequent employment. Contractionary shocks lead firms to revise employment plans downward immediately and persistently, eventually reducing employment growth. Initially, hiring plans are reduced, while layoffs increase later. Production expectations adjust twice as often but revert faster, consistent with greater labour market rigidity. Labour market institutions shape these responses: firms subject to the minimum wage or with lower collective bargaining coverage revise employment expectations more strongly. Financially constrained firms exhibit disproportionately larger downward revisions, indicating that the financial accelerator operates already at the expectation formation stage. Because firms adjust plans well before effects appear in aggregate data, employment expectations provide an early measure of monetary policy transmission to the labour market.

rejected.title: Financial frictions across the production network and the transmission of monetary policy
rejected.title_original: Financial frictions across the production network and the transmission of monetary policy
rejected.summary_original: We show that monetary policy transmission is shaped not only by a sector’s own financial frictions but also by those prevailing in the broader production network. The latter, indirect frictions amplify the output and price effects of monetary policy and empirically dominate the direct ones. The amplification results from a downstream demand channel, as customers respond to tighter policy by purchasing fewer inputs. This is partly offset by an upstream cost channel, reflecting that suppliers raise prices to protect margins when financing costs rise. We inspect the mechanism in a multi-sector general equilibrium model with input-output linkages and working-capital constraints.

rejected.summary_original: This paper introduces reduced-form macroeconometric tools, emphasising quantile regression models, to identify key risk drivers for the euro area economy and assess risks around the baseline ECB/Eurosystem staff macroeconomic projections for the euro area inflation and growth. The analysis uses a large number of risk factors, going beyond the usual financial factors, employing a sequential selection approach with robustness checks. To support the analysis a MATLAB toolbox (M@RX) was developed, incorporating several quantile regression-based model classes with a novel parametric tilting methodology and a copula approach for transforming predictive densities across frequencies. This paper contributes to the literature on the treatment of the COVID-era data in quantile regression models. Results indicate that the predictive content of risk factors is horizon, time and objective-dependent. rejected.title: Assessing the scope for compensatory fiscal measures in response to the recent energy shock
rejected.title_original: Assessing the scope for compensatory fiscal measures in response to the recent energy shock
rejected.summary_original: This box assesses the scope for euro area governments to adopt compensatory fiscal measures against the backdrop of the recent energy shock. It examines the available fiscal space, reviews the discretionary fiscal support provided so far, and assesses whether the current inflation environment has generated additional revenues that could partially finance current and future measures. The box concludes that, since fiscal space is more constrained than it was during the 2022 energy crisis and there is only modest scope for self-financing through inflation-driven revenues, it is all the more important for fiscal support to be temporary, targeted and tailored.
